Auckland to Auckland · under sail

New Zealand one coast at a time

Cast off in Auckland. Wake beneath Rangitoto. Follow the island anchorages north until Cape Reinga turns the bow toward a country that grows wilder with every mile.

You do not see New Zealand from a yacht. You arrive into it—bay by bay, headland by headland, morning by morning.

~3,000 nmAuckland to Auckland
14 monthsThe unhurried version
12 chaptersSubtropical to subantarctic
1 continuous wakeAround Aotearoa
NZ · COASTAL LOGChooseCast offRouteThe coastThe voyageThe wakeLife aboardNumbersHomecoming

The first choice

How far is the horizon calling you?

Both routes leave Auckland, round Cape Reinga, meet the other coast and return through East Cape and Aotea. One becomes a great island circuit. The other keeps going until New Zealand feels like a continent made entirely of weather, mountains and remembered arrivals.

Departure · Auckland · 05:42

The harbour is still asleep when you cast off

The engine idles past the last marina fingers. Ferries begin moving across the harbour. Rangitoto sits ahead in the blue-grey morning and, for now, the entire voyage is only the distance to the first anchorage.

You are not trying to sail around a country today. You are sailing to an island. Tonight the city will glow beyond the stern; tomorrow the Gulf will offer another bay. Northland comes later. Cape Reinga later still. The great voyage becomes imaginable because it begins with one ordinary departure.

First wakeAuckland HarbourFirst nightHauraki GulfFirst rhythmSail · anchor · walk · wait

The Gulf teaches the rhythm. Northland builds confidence. Cape Reinga turns the page. From there, the country unfolds in the order you arrive.

01Arrive differently

A harbour entered from sea has weather, approach, anticipation and relief. Places become remembered arrivals rather than points on a road.

02Carry home with you

Markets, tracks, repairs, rainy mornings and bakery raids matter as much as the sailing. The boat becomes a small address that moves.

03Close the wake

You return through the Hauraki Gulf with every cape and anchorage connected behind you. New Zealand has not become smaller. It has become personal.

The second choice

What part of the adventure speaks to you?

The complete voyage remains visible. Matching moments brighten, the strongest regions illuminate on the map and a quiet marker says: this may be the chapter that pulls you in first.

Eight changes in character

Follow the wake from harbour to harbour

The route is anticlockwise, but the story moves forward: Auckland to the Gulf, the Gulf into Northland, Northland to Cape Reinga, then south through increasingly serious water until the long return begins.

1 · Green Water2 · Coastal Confidence3 · Open-Coast Resolve4 · Serious Water5 · Edge of the Map
01 · Cast off

Auckland Harbour

Ferries cross the bow. Rangitoto holds the horizon. The first night is only a few islands away.

02 · Settle in

Hauraki Gulf → Bay of Islands

Waiheke, Kawau and Mahurangi teach the rhythm. Whangārei and the Bay of Islands make the boat feel like home.

03 · Turn the corner

Whangaroa → Cape Reinga

The anchorages thin out. The great northern cape appears. The bow turns from the Pacific toward the Tasman.

04 · Cross over

West Coast → Cook Strait

Night sailing, a long horizon, Wellington’s lights and then the narrow water between the islands.

05 · Go south

Kaikōura → Rakiura

Mountains rise from the sea. The air cools. Foveaux Strait carries you into the deep south.

06 · Reach the wild coast

Fiordland → West Coast

The yacht becomes the smallest object in the landscape. Patience becomes as important as motion.

07 · Turn toward warmth

Nelson → East Cape

The boat dries, spring arrives and each northward mile reconnects the voyage to familiar water.

08 · Close the circle

Aotea → Auckland

Rangitoto appears ahead. The same harbour returns beneath a very different wake.

How the coast changes

Not every mile asks the same of you

The colours on the route describe the character of the journey—not a forecast or a guarantee. Sheltered Gulf water gradually gives way to open coast, great straits and the remote southern edge.

Passage 1Green Water

The coastline is forgiving enough to learn the rhythm.

Passage 2Coastal Confidence

Longer days begin turning technique into instinct.

Passage 3Open-Coast Resolve

Weather, patience and judgment start carrying equal weight.

Passage 4Serious Water

Capes, straits and darkness ask for preparation—and give achievement back.

Passage 5Edge of the Map

Self-reliance becomes real, quiet and deeply earned.

Never sailed before?
You begin before the Gulf.

You do not need 3,000 miles today. You need the first lesson, the first crew day and enough curiosity to look beyond the harbour entrance. Skills accumulate in the same way this voyage does: one short stretch of water at a time.

Act I

The Harbour Door Opens

You cast off in Auckland, spend the first nights among the Gulf islands, then follow the red pōhutukawa coast north until Cape Reinga fills the horizon.

780 nmPassage 1 → 4Auckland → Cape Reinga
05:48 — the Gulf. The skyline is still visible, but the voyage has already begun.
01
The harbour door opens

Tāmaki Makaurau & the Hauraki Gulf

November · 80 nautical miles

Auckland → Rangitoto → Waiheke → Mahurangi

Passage characterLevel 1 · Green Water

You ease away from Auckland while the ferries are still building their morning wakes. Rangitoto stays off the bow; the skyline becomes smaller behind the stern. By evening the anchor is down at Motuihe, Waiheke or Mahurangi. The city lights remain visible, but the boat has become its own small address. At dawn, coffee steams in the cockpit and the first island fills the view. The journey has started without requiring the horizon to be dramatic.

From the logbook

The first night is the real departure. Sleep aboard within sight of home and the whole map begins to open.

The coastline is forgiving enough to learn the rhythm.
When the anchor is down

Swim at Motuihe, walk Waiheke’s coast, visit Kawau’s Mansion House and let Mahurangi become the first bay where you lose track of the date.

A small reward

Oneroa bread, Gulf oysters in season, and the first dinner that tastes better simply because the boat is swinging to her own anchor.

Enough reality to believe it

Auckland is the perfect place to discover the boat’s irritating habits while help is still close.

02
Confidence arrives

Te Tai Tokerau / Northland

November–December · 235 nautical miles

Hauraki Gulf → Whangārei → Bay of Islands → Whangaroa

Passage characterLevel 2 · Coastal Confidence

You leave the Gulf with the boat beginning to make sense beneath your feet. Leigh slips astern, Whangārei opens ahead and the Poor Knights sit offshore like a promise. Then the Bay of Islands appears—not as one destination, but as a whole week of possible mornings. You enter under sail, choose an anchorage by the shelter and the light, swim over the anchor and walk uphill before dinner. Farther north, Whangaroa feels carved specifically for a cruising yacht. The rhythm is no longer something you are trying to learn. It is simply how the days work.

Whangamumu
history beneath green hillsWhangaroa
the perfect waiting roomBay of Islands
too many good choices
From the logbook

Northland rewards the sailor who stops treating every bay as a waypoint and starts letting the coast set the pace.

Longer days begin turning technique into instinct.
When the anchor is down

Snorkel the Poor Knights, walk to Whangamumu’s old whaling station, wander Russell, climb above Whangaroa and give Waitangi the time it deserves.

A small reward

Mangonui fish and chips, Kerikeri fruit stalls and the last indecently large bakery order before the Far North.

Enough reality to believe it

Opua is the natural reset: groceries, fuel, repairs and one good night’s sleep before the coastline becomes less forgiving.

03
The first real test

Cape Reinga & the western horizon

January · 465 nautical miles

Far North → Cape Reinga → New Plymouth → Wellington

Passage characterLevel 4 · Serious Water

The last northern anchorage is quiet because everything ahead feels large. You leave before dawn and watch Te Rerenga Wairua take shape in the first light. At Cape Reinga the east coast ends, the Tasman begins and the bow finally turns south. Northland is now behind you as a string of remembered bays. Ahead lies a longer horizon, the first night offshore and a western coast that offers few easy interruptions. When New Plymouth and then Wellington finally appear, city lights feel less ordinary than they ever have before.

One long horizon. One wake. One coast with nowhere sensible to rush.

From the logbook

Cape Reinga does not care about your calendar. Wait until the boat, the weather and your own mind all say the same thing.

Capes, straits and darkness ask for preparation—and give achievement back.
When the anchor is down

After the empty western reach, New Plymouth’s coastal walkway and Wellington’s waterfront feel almost extravagantly civilised.

A small reward

A hot breakfast ashore after night watches may be the most memorable meal of the circuit.

Enough reality to believe it

This is the longest likely nonstop passage—about 390 nautical miles. Taking another capable sailor here is sensible, not a betrayal of the solo dream.

Act II

Beyond the Easy Harbours

Wellington’s lights appear after the long western coast. Cook Strait opens the door to Kaikōura, Canterbury and the long road south.

525 nmPassage 3 → 4Cook Strait → Otago
Four days waiting in Port Underwood. On the fifth morning, the Strait finally looks ordinary.
04
Beyond the easy harbours

Cook Strait & Kaikōura

Late January–February · 110 nautical miles

Wellington → Cook Strait → Port Underwood → Kaikōura

Passage characterLevel 4 · Serious Water

Wellington gives you laundry, hot food and several days to study the water outside the harbour. Then one morning the Strait looks ordinary. You cast off, shorten sail early and enter a moving landscape of tide, wind and traffic. Hours later Port Underwood folds around the boat and the world becomes quiet again. The next departure brings the Kaikōura ranges over the horizon—snow, cloud and ocean stacked into the same impossible view. The voyage has crossed from one island into another character entirely.

From the logbook

Shorten sail before the Strait asks. Good seamanship often looks wonderfully uneventful from the shore.

Capes, straits and darkness ask for preparation—and give achievement back.
When the anchor is down

Walk the Kaikōura Peninsula, watch seals from a respectful distance and use a weather day for whales rather than another forecast tab.

A small reward

A bowl of something hot with the ranges outside the window. Kaikōura’s name is associated with a meal of crayfish—a fitting place to eat from the coast.

Enough reality to believe it

Short in miles, serious in timing. Wellington and Port Underwood are the places to wait without apology.

05
The long eastern edge

Canterbury, Otago & the Catlins

February–March · 415 nautical miles

Kaikōura → Banks Peninsula → Otago → the Catlins

Passage characterLevel 3 · Open-Coast Resolve

You follow the mountains south until Banks Peninsula interrupts the long coast. Lyttelton feels industrious; Akaroa feels almost theatrical; Otago Harbour arrives with colder air and an unmistakable sense of latitude. Between them, the boat moves through port towns, empty beaches and metallic evening light. Groceries in Dunedin, a walk above the harbour and clean clothes briefly return life to normal. Then another southerly rattles the rigging and the chart shows Foveaux Strait waiting below the Catlins.

From the logbook

A long coast is not conquered in one heroic decision. It is sailed through a hundred sensible ones.

Weather, patience and judgment start carrying equal weight.
When the anchor is down

Climb above Lyttelton, wander Akaroa, explore Oamaru’s Victorian quarter and spend a full day in Dunedin rather than treating it as a supermarket with buildings.

A small reward

Cheese rolls in the south, good coffee in Dunedin and a bag of fresh produce that makes the cabin smell like land.

Enough reality to believe it

Lyttelton and Otago are reassuring reset points. Between them, some harbours remain possibilities rather than promises.

Act III

At the Edge of the Map

Rakiura changes the soundscape. Fiordland changes the scale. The West Coast teaches you to measure progress in weather windows rather than days.

740 nmPassage 4 → 5Rakiura → West Coast
Milford Sound, 46° south. The yacht is the smallest object in the scene.
06
The deep south

Foveaux Strait & Rakiura

March · 105 nautical miles

Bluff → Foveaux Strait → Rakiura

Passage characterLevel 4 · Serious Water

Bluff disappears behind the stern and Rakiura slowly separates itself from the weather ahead. Once inside Paterson Inlet, the soundscape changes first: fewer engines, more birds, water moving through kelp beside the hull. You carry fresh bread back from Oban in cold air, take the dinghy toward Ulva Island and return after dark beneath a sky with no city glow. The yacht seems very small here, yet the cabin light makes it feel like the most complete home you have ever owned.

Listen for: kākā over the masthead · tokoeka after dark · seabirds working Foveaux water · silence where roads should be
From the logbook

In the deep south, self-reliance stops being an idea. It becomes the warm light inside the cabin.

Capes, straits and darkness ask for preparation—and give achievement back.
When the anchor is down

Walk from Oban, visit predator-free Ulva Island, listen for tokoeka and look up into one of the world’s southern dark-sky sanctuaries.

A small reward

A warm pub, blue cod, and the particular happiness of carrying fresh bread back to the dinghy in cold air.

Enough reality to believe it

Bluff and Invercargill are the last effortless provisioning. South of Halfmoon Bay, self-sufficiency stops being decorative.

07
The reward

Fiordland northbound

Late March–April · 285 nautical miles

Rakiura → Preservation Inlet → Milford Sound

Passage characterLevel 5 · Edge of the Map

You leave Rakiura with weeks of food aboard and the western edge of the country ahead. The first fiord opens like a break in the mountains. Inside, the sea flattens, the cliffs rise and the yacht appears to stop moving because there is nothing human-sized against which to judge its speed. Rain creates waterfalls by the hundred. Mist removes the mountain tops. In a quiet cove the forest appears twice—once above the water and once below the keel. Morning begins with the kettle and the soft pull of a shore line. This is what the southern miles were carrying you toward.

From the logbook

Fiordland is the reward, but it charges in preparation. Pay gladly; few places on earth give so much back.

Self-reliance becomes real, quiet and deeply earned.
When the anchor is down

Step carefully into the history of Astronomer’s Point and Luncheon Cove, nose the dinghy toward waterfalls and let most places remain gloriously unvisited.

A small reward

Fresh bread from the pressure cooker, strong coffee and one deliberately saved meal opened while rain drums on the coachroof.

Enough reality to believe it

Four to eight weeks without dependable resupply makes Fiordland the longest truly remote chapter. The complexity belongs in the preparation, not on this page.

08
The wild coast

The South Island West Coast

April–May · 350 nautical miles

Fiordland → Jackson Bay → the South Island West Coast

Passage characterLevel 5 · Edge of the Map

The West Coast immediately takes control of the calendar. You spend seven days inside while rain sweeps the anchorage and the swell refuses to settle. Books are finished. Jobs are completed. The café owner begins recognising the wet jacket. Then the front passes, the sea arranges itself into long lines and two moving days appear on the forecast. You leave at first light and sail north beneath a scrubbed-blue sky, surf booming along an empty shore. The waiting has not interrupted the voyage. It has made this departure possible.

Day 1 RainDay 3 SwellDay 5 Boat jobsDay 7 The sea settlesDays 8–9 350 miles of earned motion
From the logbook

The West Coast owns the timetable. Sailors who accept that are the ones who eventually get to move.

Self-reliance becomes real, quiet and deeply earned.
When the anchor is down

Find a hot meal in Jackson Bay, greenstone and art in Hokitika, West Coast history in Greymouth and limestone country near Punakaiki when transport and weather align.

A small reward

Whitebait in season, a West Coast pie and anything warm enough to fog a café window.

Enough reality to believe it

Few refuges and changing river bars make this the second place where temporary crew can increase enjoyment rather than merely reduce risk.

Act IV

The Long Way Home

Nelson brings warmth and people back into the story. Then Wairarapa, East Cape, Coromandel and Aotea lead you toward the harbour where the wake began.

815 nmPassage 4 → 2Nelson → Auckland
The light grows warmer. Distances that once looked enormous now carry names and memories.
09
Winter light

Golden Bay, Nelson & the Sounds

May–August · 190 nautical miles

Golden Bay → Nelson → Marlborough Sounds

Passage characterLevel 2 · Coastal Confidence

The first Nelson market bag feels almost absurdly luxurious after the West Coast. The boat dries. Clothes become clothes again instead of damp categories. Repairs are made by people with workshops; coffee arrives in cups that do not slide across the table. You settle into winter rather than merely waiting through it—short sails inside the Sounds, long walks above the anchorages and silver light reaching between the hills. For a while, the voyage becomes a neighbourhood.

Market bags in the dinghy · clean laundry · a repaired autopilot · familiar faces at the counter · winter sunlight between the hills
From the logbook

A wise sailor knows when a harbour is not a delay, but a whole season worth living.

Longer days begin turning technique into instinct.
When the anchor is down

Walk pieces of the Abel Tasman and Queen Charlotte tracks, browse Nelson Market, explore D’Urville and eat green-shell mussels near Havelock.

A small reward

Nelson market produce, Marlborough mussels and the dangerous discovery of a favourite bakery within walking distance of the dinghy.

Enough reality to believe it

This is the obvious winter pause and maintenance reset—civilisation without abandoning the voyage.

10
Turning north

Wairarapa & Hawke’s Bay

September–October · 175 nautical miles

Wellington → Cape Palliser → Wairarapa → Napier

Passage characterLevel 3 · Open-Coast Resolve

You leave the Sounds in spring and cross Cook Strait again, but the water no longer feels like the same frontier. Wellington is now a place you have arrived twice. Cape Palliser slides astern and the bow points north along Wairarapa. Days lengthen; the temperature lifts by degrees. When Napier’s palms and precise Art Deco streets appear, they look wonderfully improbable after months of forest, rain and steep-sided sounds. Home is still far away, but it has finally become a direction.

From the logbook

Turning north does not make the coast smaller. It shows you how much larger your own scale has become.

Weather, patience and judgment start carrying equal weight.
When the anchor is down

Return to Wellington as an old acquaintance, walk Castlepoint only in settled weather and give Napier’s Art Deco streets a day free of errands.

A small reward

Hawke’s Bay fruit, a vineyard lunch if the budget forgives it, and the first outdoor coffee that actually feels warm.

Enough reality to believe it

If spring remains boisterous, the Marlborough Sounds are a much better place to wait than the exposed Wairarapa coast.

11
The sunward coast

Hawke’s Bay, East Cape & Bay of Plenty

October–November · 260 nautical miles

Hawke’s Bay → East Cape → Bay of Plenty

Passage characterLevel 4 · Serious Water

Hawke’s Bay opens into long eastern reaches where you anchor only because the night has been kind enough to allow it. The first sunlight in the country finds the cockpit before breakfast. Gisborne brings produce and people; Tolaga Bay brings a long walk over the water; East Cape brings another headland slowly passing into the wake. Then the Bay of Plenty widens ahead and summer returns in the colour of the sea. Meals move back into the cockpit. Bare feet reappear. Auckland begins to feel near enough to postpone.

From the logbook

An open roadstead at dawn is a gift with an expiry time. Take the beauty seriously—and the forecast more seriously still.

Capes, straits and darkness ask for preparation—and give achievement back.
When the anchor is down

Walk Tolaga Bay’s extraordinary wharf, visit Tairāwhiti Museum, climb Mauao and seek the small coastal places that make more sense from a boat than from a highway.

A small reward

Gisborne produce, roadside citrus and fish eaten outside because the cabin is finally too warm.

Enough reality to believe it

Napier, Gisborne and Tauranga make the dream believable. Between them, open bays are gifts from the forecast rather than permanent refuges.

12
Homeward with 3,000 miles behind you

Coromandel, Aotea & home

November–December · 190 nautical miles

Coromandel → Aotea → Waiheke → Auckland

Passage characterLevel 2 · Coastal Confidence

Mercury Bay, Coromandel and Aotea return you to warm island water, but none of it feels like the coast you once knew. Every familiar headland now connects to another one far beyond it. The yacht has her routines; you know when to reef, when to wait and when to let a beautiful anchorage steal another day. Auckland is close enough to reach, so you spend one final night at Waiheke instead. In the morning Rangitoto rises ahead, the skyline appears beyond it and the track around the country closes beneath the keel.

The skyline that once meant departure now means completion.

From the logbook

Do not hurry the final twenty miles. Home will still be there after one more night at anchor.

Longer days begin turning technique into instinct.
When the anchor is down

Walk the Aotea Track, soak at Kaitoke Hot Springs, climb Hirakimata, explore Coromandel history and finish with an unreasonably slow lunch on Waiheke.

A small reward

Fresh bread, island coffee and a bottle saved since Bluff—opened only when the skyline finally appears.

Enough reality to believe it

The same harbour returns. The sailor does not.

The Other Side

Now look back along the wake

Twelve moments worth sailing 3,000 miles for

After travelling the route in order, these are the scenes that remain: the mornings, arrivals and horizons that make every damp sock, delayed departure and grocery-laden dinghy ride worthwhile.

01Passage 1 · Green Water

Wake beneath Rangitoto while Auckland is still asleep.

Perhaps next year…

Beyond this voyage

The North Island loop closes in Auckland—but the track does not have to end there. South of Cook Strait waits an entirely different journey: Kaikōura, Rakiura, Fiordland, the West Coast and the Sounds. Some sailors continue. Others return with a larger boat, another season and a much longer list of reasons to leave again.

Three perfect days

The voyage between the passages

The circumnavigation is sold by capes and miles. It is remembered through mornings when the boat goes nowhere at all.

Port Fitzroy · Aotea

Warm water and high tracks

  1. Dawn coffee while the inlet is still polished flat.
  2. Walk ashore before the heat reaches the ridges.
  3. Swim over the anchor and inspect it because you can.
  4. Fresh bread, an early dinner and the evening forecast in the cockpit.

Paterson Inlet · Rakiura

Birdsong instead of roads

  1. Listen for kākā before leaving the bunk.
  2. Dinghy ashore for forest and an Ulva Island visit.
  3. Return with cold hands and something fresh from Oban.
  4. Watch the southern darkness arrive without a single city glow.

Marlborough Sounds

Winter sunlight

  1. A short sail after breakfast rather than before it.
  2. Walk a piece of the Queen Charlotte Track.
  3. Complete one satisfying boat job in dry clothes.
  4. Green-shell mussels, a book and absolutely no departure alarm.

Life between the capes

What a week aboard feels like

It is not seven consecutive days of heroic sailing. It is a floating life in which motion, waiting, maintenance and discovery take turns.

Monday

Forty miles sailed and dinner at anchor.

Tuesday

Rain, reading and engine maintenance.

Wednesday

Walked to a viewpoint above the bay.

Thursday

Waited for the wind to turn.

Friday

Left before sunrise; rounded the cape by lunch.

Saturday

Groceries, laundry and an indecent bakery order.

Sunday

Went nowhere—and it was the best day of the week.

A solo voyage with a cast

The people who become part of the voyage

Solo rarely means untouched by other lives. Some people appear for ten minutes; years later, their sentence is still aboard.

✎

“Not there. Here.”

The local sailor redraws your anchoring plan on a paper napkin.
⌁

The information you actually needed

A harbourmaster replaces five anxious assumptions with one useful fact.
⚙

Ten minutes to find the fault

The mechanic listens, reaches behind the engine and makes the impossible look obvious.
≈

What the swell is doing outside

A fisherman describes tomorrow’s sea with the confidence of someone who met today’s at dawn.
☕

“The usual?”

On the fourth weather day, the café owner recognises both you and your wet jacket.
↗

One difficult coast shared

A temporary crewmate joins for the miles you never needed to prove alone.

The weather day is still part of the voyage

Waiting well is not dead time. It is how the route acquires places and people that were never on the original plan.

☕

📖

🌤

Find the unplanned favourite

Five rituals that become the year

A voyage is made believable by repetition

The landmarks change. These small acts quietly turn an unfamiliar yacht and coastline into a life.

01

Coffee before the forecast.

02

Looking over the stern after the anchor settles.

03

Reefing earlier than seems necessary.

04

Walking uphill whenever weather keeps the boat still.

05

Writing down where the day ended.

Gentle honesty

This is not always the postcard

Wet clothingBroken sleepLong weather waitsExpensive repairsMotoring in no windTurning backLonelinessArriving too tired to appreciate it
None of these diminish the voyage. They are part of why completing it means something.
Planning-scale figures are approximate. Before any real voyage, use current LINZ charts and tides, MetService marine forecasts, Maritime NZ guidance, harbourmaster information and current DOC/biosecurity rules. This guide is an invitation—not pilotage.

Before Auckland ever falls astern

Your first mile is closer than 3,000

You do not need to own the yacht, understand every forecast or know whether Fiordland will ever appear over your bow. You only need to begin becoming the sailor who could one day make that choice.

The first afternoon

Feel the boat answer

A lesson turns invisible wind into movement. The mystery becomes a skill you can practise.

The first crew day

Borrow experience

Sail with people who know more. Hear the stories, learn the habits and discover that capable sailors are made, not born.

The first dawn afloat

Let the map change

Wake at anchor once and every headland becomes an opening instead of an edge.

The voyage begins long before the lines are cast off. It begins the day “one day” becomes “I’m learning.”

The quiet transformation

What the voyage changes

No grand reinvention. Just a collection of small recalibrations that follow you back through the harbour entrance.

A thirty-mile sail stops feeling far.

Waiting becomes an active decision.

A dry bunk becomes a luxury.

Cities are judged partly by their dinghy landings.

Weather becomes something lived rather than checked.

Home is no longer the place you never left.

New Zealand changes from a coastline into hundreds of remembered arrivals.

Auckland again

The same harbour.
Not the same sailor.

The skyline appears where the journey began. The harbour is familiar, but your scale of distance has changed. Places that once felt remote now carry memories: a bay entered at dusk, a headland waited behind for four days, a southern anchorage where the mountains disappeared into rain. The track around the country closes behind you. New Zealand has not become smaller. It has become personal.
